title: Nehemiah 1:4–11
context: Nehemiah 1:4–11 records Nehemiah’s response: he weeps, mourns for days, fasts, and prays before the God of heaven, and the prayer is kept here as one unit. It addresses the LORD as the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness, in language close to Deuteronomy 7:9 and Daniel 9:4. It asks God to hear, confesses the sins of Israel including Nehemiah’s own house, and appeals to the word given through Moses that God would scatter his people for unfaithfulness and gather them if they returned (compare Deuteronomy 30:1–4). It recalls that they are the people God redeemed by his great power and strong hand, and it ends with a request for success and mercy before “this man”, whom the closing line identifies by implication as the king Nehemiah served as cup bearer. Both traditions read the confession and the covenant language as largely shared ground: God is faithful to his word, his people are guilty and dependent on his mercy, and repentance and prayer are the right response. How prayer relates to God’s purposes is already treated in the existing box at Joshua 10:14, and questions about the perseverance of God’s people are treated at 1 Samuel 12:22; neither is reopened here.

verses.text: When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and mourned several days; and I fasted and prayed before the God of heaven,
verses.arminianNotes:
When Nehemiah hears these words, he sits down and weeps, mourns for several days, and fasts and prays before the God of heaven. Grief becomes prayer.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah’s sorrow is sincere and costly, and they see him choosing to bring his grief to God rather than despairing, a model of honest lament joined to persistent seeking.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the title God of heaven, which appears often in Ezra and Nehemiah, confesses that the God of Israel rules over all, including the empire Nehemiah serves, and they see his fasting as humble dependence on that sovereign God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and do not use it to reopen the question, treated at Joshua 10:14, of how prayer relates to God’s purposes.

verses.text: and said, “I beg you, LORD, the God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments,
verses.arminianNotes:
He begins, “I beg you, LORD, the God of heaven, the great and awesome God who keeps covenant and loving kindness with those who love him and keep his commandments”. The language is close to Deuteronomy 7:9 and Daniel 9:4.

Arminian readers note that the description joins God’s faithfulness with the response of those who love and obey him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the prayer begins with God’s character and covenant faithfulness before making any request, and they see the confession of God as great and awesome as the ground of confidence in prayer.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God keeps covenant and loving kindness, and his people are called to love him and keep his commandments.

verses.text: let your ear now be attentive and your eyes open, that you may listen to the prayer of your servant which I pray before you at this time, day and night, for the children of Israel your servants, while I confess the sins of the children of Israel which we have sinned against you. Yes, I and my father’s house have sinned.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah asks God to let his ear be attentive and his eyes open to the prayer of his servant, prayed day and night for the children of Israel, while he confesses the sins of the people, including his own and his father’s house.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah includes himself in the confession, taking personal responsibility rather than blaming others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the request for God’s attentive ear as echoing Solomon’s prayer (compare 1 Kings 8:29, 52), and they note that confession of sin is the honest posture of those who approach a holy God.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about corporate and personal confession, persistent prayer, and the humility that belongs to God’s servants.

verses.text: We have dealt very corruptly against you, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the ordinances, which you commanded your servant Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
He confesses, “We have dealt very corruptly against you, and have not kept the commandments, nor the statutes, nor the ordinances, which you commanded your servant Moses.” The confession is frank.

Arminian readers note that the people’s failure is described as real disobedience to known commands, for which they are responsible, and they see repentance as the right and possible response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the confession makes no excuse and appeals to no merit, and they see it as an acknowledgment that the people stand before God only on the basis of his mercy.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: honest confession names sin plainly and looks to God’s mercy rather than to human worth.

verses.text: “Remember, I beg you, the word that you commanded your servant Moses, saying, ‘If you trespass, I will scatter you among the peoples;
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks God to remember the word commanded to Moses: if they trespass, God will scatter them among the peoples. The warning recalls passages such as Leviticus 26:33, “I will scatter you among the nations”.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah appeals to God’s word as a faithful and conditional warning, now fulfilled in the exile, which shows that God’s warnings are real.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Nehemiah appeals to God’s own word rather than to the people’s deserving, and they see in the fulfilled warning a reason to trust that the promise attached to it will also be kept.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s faithfulness to his word in judgment and in mercy.

verses.text: but if you return to me, and keep my commandments and do them, though your outcasts were in the uttermost part of the heavens, yet I will gather them from there, and will bring them to the place that I have chosen, to cause my name to dwell there.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The cited word continues: if they return and keep God’s commandments, even if their outcasts are at the uttermost part of the heavens, God will gather them and bring them to the place he has chosen to cause his name to dwell there. Compare Deuteronomy 30:1–4 and 12:11.

Arminian readers note the call to return as a real invitation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the gathering is God’s work, from as far as the uttermost part of the heavens, and they see the promise as resting on God’s choice of the place for his name.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: God calls his people to return and promises to gather them, and Nehemiah’s prayer rests on that promise.

verses.text: “Now these are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah says, “Now these are your servants and your people, whom you have redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.” The prayer echoes Moses’ intercession (compare Deuteronomy 9:29).

Arminian readers note that the appeal rests on the relationship God established with his people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that God has already redeemed this people by his power, and they see Nehemiah pleading God’s own past work as the reason he should act again for them, since the people belong to him.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s redemption of his people and the confidence it gives in prayer, without turning it into a debate about election.

verses.text: Lord, I beg you, let your ear be attentive now to the prayer of your servant, and to the prayer of your servants who delight to fear your name; and please prosper your servant today, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Now I was cup bearer to the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
He asks the Lord to attend to his prayer and to the prayers of his servants who delight to fear his name, and to prosper his servant today and grant him mercy in the sight of this man; the verse adds that Nehemiah was cup bearer to the king.

Arminian readers see Nehemiah preparing to act, asking God’s help for a real and risky decision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Nehemiah prays for favor in the king’s heart, confident that God can turn a ruler’s mind, and they see his position as cup bearer as part of God’s providential preparation.

Both traditions read the closing request as shared ground: prayer and responsible action belong together, and the outcome rests with God.
